name: East Slopes
approach: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, at the end of White River Road/FR 6400, reached via WA-207 and White River Road from Coles Corner off US-2), follow the White River Trail (#1507) upstream along a mostly level grade through old-growth forest for about 4 miles to its junction with the Boulder Pass Trail (#1562, also called the Boulder Creek Trail). Water is abundant the whole way — the White River parallels the trail, and Boulder Creek is a dependable source at the junction (the crossing here can be a ford depending on the year/season, so check recent trip reports before committing). Turn onto the Boulder Pass Trail and climb switchbacks through forest, gaining roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about 3 miles to break out into the open basin below Boulder Pass (~5,000 ft). Because the round trip from the trailhead runs in the 20+ mile range with well over 6,000 ft of gain, most parties do this as an overnight, camping in the Boulder Pass basin or pushing on to a high camp in Upper Boulder Basin (~5,800 ft). From the basin, leave the maintained trail for the unmaintained 'sheepherder's path,' a boot track that sidehills east across a series of cirques (Clark Basin, then Luahna Basin), losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining elevation near a 7,200 ft spur. This traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or snow cover. From the spur, a rising traverse across broad benches (often snow-covered well into summer) and easy Class 2 ledges leads to the ~7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain; from there a rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier (real crevasse hazard — carry glacier travel gear, and note the glacier has been reported thinning/broken-up and less straightforward in recent years) reaches Luahna's East Ridge, which is scrambled west to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the sheepherder's traverse to the col west of Clark Mountain, then the upper Richardson Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft at the end of FR-6400, White River Trail #1507 runs almost level upstream through old growth for about four miles. The junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562 sits roughly a quarter mile past the bridge over Boulder Creek — if you have crossed the creek and seen no sign, keep walking. Turn onto #1562 and climb gently through forest to the established camp at the creek crossing near 3,700 ft; whether that is a step-across or a genuine ford depends on the year. Above camp the trail switchbacks and climbs roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about three miles into the open basin below Boulder Pass. Snow lingers in that basin well into summer, and the pass is the last of the maintained, easy-to-follow trail. Above Boulder Pass the route becomes an unmaintained sheepherder's path that sidehills east across a series of cirques, losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining height near a 7,200 ft spur. That traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach: brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or under snow. This route also carries a set of waypoints describing a different line — over the pass, down to a ford of the Napeequa near 4,700 ft, and up to a high basin at 7,000 ft under the east face. Both are real ways to this mountain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable. The Richardson has been reported thinning and breaking up in recent years, so a late-season party should expect it to be less straightforward than it used to be
hazards: Crevasses and moats on an upper Richardson Glacier that recent parties report thinning and breaking up
The sheepherder's traverse across the cirques — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in cloud or snow
A short low Class 4 step below the east ridge that can carry verglas and has no fixed anchor
Loose scree and rotten rock just below the summit block
A Thunder Creek exit that reads shorter on the map and is documented as slower, brushier and harder to follow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival at the climbing is a glacier, and the thing that gets you to it is a col that belongs to the next peak. From the 7,200 ft spur, make a rising traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy Class 2 ledges to the roughly 7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain. You are navigating to a gap beside a different summit, which is what makes it findable: Clark is the big thing on your left.

From that col, the route is one rising traverse across the Upper Richardson Glacier to Luahna's east ridge. Rope up at the col. The glacier crossing is the route; the ridge above it is a scramble west to the summit.

The critical negative marker is about which glacier you are on, and this peak's own record has already been wrong about it once: the Pilz and Butterfly Glaciers are on Luahna's north slope and belong to a separate route approached from the Napeequa side. This route uses the Richardson, which lies to the south-east of the summit. If the glacier you have stepped onto is north of the peak, you are on the other mountain's business entirely.

The second negative marker is simpler: if you never touched a glacier at all, you are on the south-west slopes and south-east ridge line, which is the other route on this peak and is deliberately glacier-free. Both finish on the same summit and neither is a variation of the other.

Coming down, the one piece of technical ground is below the east ridge: a short, steep step reported as low Class 4 and sometimes verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties downclimb it; a single 20-30 m rappel off a horn or block is common practice when it is wet or icy. There is no fixed anchor — carry webbing.

Do not take the thunder creek exit on the strength of the map. Dropping south into Thunder Creek looks shorter and is reported slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown, avalanche debris and a boot path that disappears near the creek crossing. Reversing the ascent line over Boulder Pass is the reliable way out.

waypoints.name: White River Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk and Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee required; vault toilet, no potable water on site.
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at Coles Corner, drive WA 207 north about 10.5 miles and turn right onto White River Road (FR 6400). Follow it about 10 miles to its end, passing Tall Timbers Ranch and keeping left at the unsigned fork beyond it, to the trailhead at about 2,300 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: White River / Boulder Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave White River Trail #1507 and turn right (east) onto Boulder Creek Trail #1562 toward Boulder Pass.
waypoints.directions: The White River Trail #1507 runs almost level upstream through old-growth forest for about four miles, with the river alongside the whole way. The junction sits roughly a quarter mile past the bridge over Boulder Creek — if you have crossed the creek and seen no sign yet, keep walking.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek ford camp
waypoints.note: Established creekside camp in deep forest near a Boulder Creek crossing, a common first-night stop for Luahna/Clark parties.
waypoints.directions: Turn onto Boulder Creek Trail #1562 and climb gently through deep forest alongside the creek to the established camp at the crossing. Whether this is a step-across or a genuine ford depends on the year and the flow, so look at it before committing to a late-day arrival.

waypoints.name: Boulder Pass
waypoints.note: High point of Boulder Creek Trail (~4,000 ft gain from the trailhead); scenic pass camping and the gateway down into the Napeequa drainage.
waypoints.directions: Above camp the trail steepens into switchbacks and climbs roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about three miles, breaking out of the forest into the open basin below the pass. Snow lingers in that basin well into summer. The pass is the last of the maintained, easy-to-follow trail.

waypoints.name: Napeequa River ford
waypoints.note: Unbridged crossing of the Napeequa River across a brushy, unmaintained valley bottom; can run high and dangerous with snowmelt, and the route is easy to lose.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and lose about 1,600 ft to the valley floor. The Napeequa bottom is unmaintained, brushy, and genuinely hard to follow in places — expect bushwhacking rather than tread. There is no bridge: scout up and down for a braided or log crossing, and cross early in the morning when overnight cold has dropped the flow.

waypoints.name: High basin below Luahna's east slopes
waypoints.note: Leave the Napeequa valley floor and climb into the open high basins under Luahna's east face, where the east-facing scree/talus ascent to the summit block begins.
waypoints.directions: Leave the valley floor and climb steeply out of the brush onto open scree and talus benches under the peak's east face, gaining roughly 2,300 ft. There is no tread here — pick a line that gets you out of the alder and onto solid ground early, because the lower slopes are the worst of it.

waypoints.name: Luahna Peak
waypoints.note: True summit on schist bedrock; Class 3 scrambling on the final block, with the Richardson Glacier just southeast and the Pilz/Butterfly Glaciers on the north slope.
